home.hero_body: A family name that means 'from Flanders' — unremarkable to Belgians, and quietly profound to the Americans who carry it. This is the story of how a milling family from East Flanders became part of the American story.

about.intro_body: What began as a search for an astronomer's unknown origins became one of the most rewarding research journeys of our lives. Our father never knew where his family came from. We do now.
about.project_body: We have traced the Van Vlaenderen line through 40+ East Flanders parishes, from a documented miller in 1568 Ghent to Charles Louis Van Vlaenderen, who left Bassevelde for America in 1881. Along the way we have worked with Flemish archives, DNA science, and the generosity of researchers on both sides of the Atlantic.
about.tools_body: Our research draws on Flemish civil and parish records, archival collections at Rijksarchief Gent and Rijksarchief Brugge, Y-DNA analysis, and AI-assisted paleography of 16th–17th century secretary hand.
about.festival_note: We first encountered the Van Vlaenderen name on a promotional banner at the Festival van Vlaenderen — a small, surreal moment that set everything in motion.
about.lineage_cta_body: We have traced 14 generations of the Van Vlaenderen family through East Flanders parish records, civil archives, and DNA analysis. Click below to see the interactive family tree.
about.contributor_michael: Michael — research, technology, and American family records
about.contributor_constance: Constance — co-researcher and family memory keeper

history.ghent_body: The earliest documented ancestor is Franciscus Van Vlaenderen, recorded in Sint-Salvator parish, Ghent, in 1568. A weaver turned miller, his family's movement from the city to the rural parishes of East Flanders over the following generations reflects the broader patterns of Flemish rural life.
history.eastflanders_body: For nearly three centuries the family worked the land and mills of parishes including Bassevelde, Oostwinkel, Boekhoute, and Waarschoot. The Van Vlaenderen name appears consistently in baptism, marriage, and burial records across this network of villages.
history.charles_body: In 1881, Charles Louis Van Vlaenderen — born in Bassevelde in 1854 — emigrated to America. He married Jacqueline Vermaas, a Dutch immigrant, and built a life in the New World. It is his branch that carries the name in America today.
history.noble_body: A separate and unproven hypothesis traces a possible line back to Victor van Vlaenderen, a documented natural son of Louis II de Male, Count of Flanders, who died before 1442 and held the lordship of Wessegem. We present this as what it is: an intriguing possibility, not a proven connection.
history.noble_caveat: Speculative — not yet supported by documentary evidence

mill.intro_body: The mill is more than a landmark — it is the thread that connects generations. The Van Vlaenderen family were millers, and the mill at the heart of Bassevelde carries their name still.
mill.visit_body: The mill remains standing in Bassevelde and is a touchstone for anyone tracing this family's roots.

dna.intro_body: Y-DNA testing can reveal connections that paper records cannot. If you carry the Van Vlaenderen surname — or a variant — your DNA may be part of this story.
dna.what_body: We are seeking male-line Van Vlaenderen descendants willing to take a Big Y-700 test. Autosomal DNA (AncestryDNA, 23andMe) is useful for close relationships but cannot confirm a shared paternal line across many generations. Y-DNA can.
dna.privacy_body: Participation is entirely voluntary. Your results are your own. We will never share individual results without explicit permission.

contact.intro_body: Whether you share the name, carry a family story, or simply want to know more — we would love to hear from you.
contact.privacy_note: We respect your privacy. Your details will never be shared or used for any purpose other than responding to you.
contact.success_message: Thank you — we will be in touch.
